name: Artie
license: Proprietary managed service. Its writer, Artie Transfer, was published on GitHub under the source-available Elastic License 2.0 from 2023, but that repository is no longer public (404 in October 2026); the Terraform provider and CLI are MIT
summary: A managed change data capture service that copies every insert, update and delete from production databases into a warehouse, aiming for under a minute of delay.
intro: An Artie pipeline has two halves. A source reader connects to your database and follows its transaction log: logical replication of the write-ahead log for PostgreSQL, the binlog for MySQL, change streams for MongoDB and DocumentDB, DynamoDB Streams, or PlanetScale’s VStream API. Every change goes into an internal Kafka topic. A writer reads that topic, keeps changes in memory and collapses several changes to the same primary key into one. When a flush rule fires (enough seconds, rows or bytes), it writes the batch to the destination as an idempotent upsert or `MERGE`, then commits its Kafka offset. A new table starts with a backfill that scans it in batches, optionally from a read replica, while live changes wait in Kafka and are applied once the scan finishes. One reader can feed several pipelines, so the database is read once for Snowflake and S3 alike. Table settings add a history table that records every change as a row, soft deletes, and column exclusion or hashing.

Artie always hosts the control plane: dashboard, configuration and monitoring. The data plane runs in Artie’s cloud in your region or, on the Enterprise plan, inside your own cloud account (bring your own cloud), where you provide Kubernetes, Kafka and storage and Artie operates it remotely. You configure it in the dashboard, through a REST API, a Terraform provider or an MCP server. Billing counts rows changed after the first backfill; backfills are free. As of October 2026 the Free plan covers 1 million rows a month and two pipelines, Growth starts at $500 a month billed annually, and Enterprise, which adds Oracle, SQL Server, Iceberg and Delta Lake, is priced by quote.
strengths: No Debezium, Kafka cluster or merge code to run yourself: Artie operates the reader, the buffer and the writes into the warehouse
Backfills run alongside live replication and never count toward the bill
One source reader can feed several destinations, so a Postgres replication slot or MySQL binlog is read only once
Warehouse-friendly writes: changes are deduplicated per key before each batched merge, with history tables and soft deletes available as table settings
limits: A closed service from a young company (founded 2023, about $15M raised by early 2026). The Transfer source it once published is no longer public, so there is no self-hosted fallback outside an Enterprise contract
It copies tables rather than transforming them: in-flight options are column-level (exclude, hash, encrypt), so joins and modelling still happen downstream, for example in dbt
Databases only, plus an events API: no SaaS-app connectors, and Oracle, SQL Server, Iceberg, Delta Lake and MySQL destinations need the Enterprise plan
Log-based CDC still costs the source something: a stalled Postgres replication slot keeps WAL until the disk fills, so the docs ask you to set heartbeats and `max_slot_wal_keep_size`
Rows bigger than the internal Kafka message limit (2 MB by default) are skipped unless you turn on message compression

story: Robin Tang had built change-data pipelines twice before Artie. At a startup acquired by Zendesk, CDC and Kafka were part of the core architecture. At Opendoor he assembled streaming pipelines from Debezium, Kafka, custom merge logic and schema inference, and after a year of work, observability and recovery from odd edge cases were still missing. Meanwhile most companies still loaded their warehouses with batch jobs every few hours or overnight.

In 2022 he started building his own replication tool, and in early 2023 he launched Artie with Jacqueline Cheong, a former investor in public software companies, who took on the business side. The first public piece, Artie Transfer, was a Go service under the Elastic License that read Debezium change events from Kafka and merged them into Snowflake. Artie joined Y Combinator’s Summer 2023 batch. Its first customer, Substack, went from warehouse data hours old to 10 to 15 seconds behind.

Since then Artie has replaced the do-it-yourself parts with its own readers and a hosted Kafka buffer, added more warehouses and lakes, raised a $3.3M seed (2024) and a $12M Series A (2026), and opened a free plan. The Transfer repository, public with about 800 stars in early 2026, is no longer visible.

choices.choice: Kafka between the reader and the writer
choices.why: The reader can keep pace with the database even when a warehouse is slow. Changes queue up during a backfill, and a pipeline paused for writing only can resume within 14 days without a new backfill.

Warehouses handle a few large merges far better than a stream of single-row updates. Collapsing repeated changes to one row before each flush cuts the volume written, and Artie argues small continuous merges use less Snowflake compute than bulk loads every hour or two.

choices.choice: Bill changed rows, not table size
choices.why: Charging only for rows processed after the first snapshot makes backfills and re-syncs free, so fixing a broken table doesn’t cost extra.
The Elastic License 2.0 let anyone read, run and modify Transfer but forbade offering it as a hosted service, which kept the managed product protected.
